setDifferenceIdentity.prompt: Let A and B be sets. Prove the equality A ∖ (A ∖ B) = A ∩ B formally using the definitions of set difference and intersection.
setDifferenceIdentity.proofIntro: Let x be an arbitrary element. Rewrite membership in the first set using the definitions:

steps.definition: Definition of set difference: x belongs to A and does not belong to A minus B.
steps.negation: Substitute the definition of A minus B and negate the conjunction.
steps.deMorgan: By De Morgan's law, the negated conjunction becomes a disjunction.
steps.simplify: Since we already know x belongs to A, x cannot be outside A; what remains is x belonging to B.
steps.intersection: By the definition of intersection, x belongs to both A and B exactly when x belongs to A intersect B.

setDifferenceIdentity.conclusion: We obtained the same membership condition for every x. By extensionality, the two sets are equal.
setDifferenceIdentity.diagramsIntro: Both diagrams highlight the part common to A and B: removing from A the part outside B leaves exactly the intersection.
setDifferenceIdentity.diagramTitle: Diagram of the shared region for {{expression}}

setMembership.duplicateNote: Since A = {1, 2}, the element A is the same set as {1, 2}. Repeated elements are counted only once in a set, so the distinct elements of B are {1, 2}, {1}, and {2}.
setMembership.task: For each statement, decide whether it is true or false.
setMembership.diagramCaption: The sets that are elements of B appear inside it; the outside numbers are elements of those sets, but not elements of B.

explanations.a: True: 1 is one of the two elements of A = {1, 2}.
explanations.b: False: the only element of {2} is the number 2. For {2} to be a subset of B, 2 would have to belong to B; B contains the set {2}, not the number 2.
explanations.c: True: the set {1} appears among the elements of B.
explanations.d: False: 2 is a number, while the elements of B are sets. In particular, {2} belongs to B, but 2 does not.
explanations.e: True: {2}, considered as a set, is one of the elements of B.
explanations.f: True: the only element of {{2}} is the set {2}, which belongs to B. Therefore every element of {{2}} belongs to B.
explanations.g: False: the elements of A are the numbers 1 and 2, and neither is a direct element of B.
explanations.h: False: the elements of {1, 2} are 1 and 2. For it to be a subset of B, both would have to belong to B, but B contains the sets {1} and {2}, not the numbers 1 and 2.
explanations.i: False: a proper subset must first be a subset, but A ⊆ B is false because 1 and 2 do not belong to B.
explanations.j: False: {1, 2} is not even a subset of B, so it cannot be a proper subset.
explanations.k: True: A = {1, 2}, and the set {1, 2} is an element of B. Therefore A ∈ B.

physics.title: Physics
physics.subtitle: Fundamental laws of nature, motion and energy.
physics.overview:
Classical physics provides a quantitative description of natural phenomena based on a small number of fundamental principles, expressed through precise mathematical relations.

The study begins with the introduction of the mathematical tools necessary for physical modeling, including scalar and vector quantities, differential and integral calculus, and ordinary differential equations of first and second order. These tools allow physical quantities to be defined operationally and related through well-defined physical laws.

The core of the subject is classical mechanics, where the motion of bodies is described within well-defined reference frames. Kinematics addresses the geometrical aspects of motion through the concepts of position, velocity, and acceleration, while dynamics establishes the connection between motion and its causes through Newton’s laws.

The treatment is extended from single particles to systems of particles and rigid bodies, introducing rotational motion, moments of inertia, rolling motion, collisions, and oscillatory phenomena.

The final part of the subject concerns thermodynamics, where macroscopic systems are described in terms of state variables and transformations, culminating in the concepts of entropy and irreversibility.

related.systems: Systems of Particles and Rigid Bodies

cybersecurity.title: Cybersecurity
cybersecurity.subtitle: Fundamental principles of computer and information security.
cybersecurity.overview:
Cybersecurity provides a systematic treatment of the fundamental principles of computer and information security, with particular emphasis on the protection of information and distributed systems. The discipline is framed within the context of information systems and is grounded in the core security objectives of confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

The concepts of risk, threats, vulnerabilities, and attack vectors are introduced, together with models for risk analysis and conceptual tools for security evaluation. It addresses authentication, authorization, and access control mechanisms, analyzing discretionary, mandatory, and role-based models.

A central part is devoted to formal security models and security policies, including classical models such as Bell–LaPadula, Biba, Clark–Wilson, and the Chinese Wall model, as well as secure design principles and their implications for the construction of trustworthy systems. The role of cryptography in system security is also introduced, covering symmetric and asymmetric encryption, digital signatures, public key infrastructures, and authentication protocols.

It further explores principles of secure design and defensive programming, analyzing major classes of software vulnerabilities and mitigation techniques. Common threats and attacks are examined, including various forms of malware, denial-of-service attacks, and social engineering techniques.

The treatment extends to network security, addressing secure network architectures, the use of cryptography for protecting communications, and defense mechanisms such as firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and traffic monitoring. Finally, advanced topics are introduced, including identity management, operating system and container security, and the foundations of smart contract and blockchain security.

dataStructures.title: Algorithms and Data Structures
dataStructures.subtitle: Design, analysis and structures for efficient data processing.
dataStructures.overview:
Algorithms and data structures introduces the fundamental principles for the design and analysis of efficient algorithms and the data structures used to organize information. The treatment begins with the formal definition of an algorithm and the study of complexity analysis criteria, introducing the concept of a fundamental operation, problem size, and Big-O notation, with particular attention to worst-case and average-case complexity, both in time and space.

Elementary internal data structures, such as arrays and linked lists, are then analyzed, focusing on their main operations and computational complexity. On this basis, abstract data structures are introduced, including stacks, queues, priority queues, and trees, as conceptual models for algorithm design.

It subsequently addresses search algorithms, including binary search, binary search trees and their balanced variants, such as AVL and 2–3 trees, as well as digital search techniques based on tries and randomized search methods.

A central part is devoted to sorting algorithms, analyzing both elementary algorithms and more efficient methods such as Quicksort, Mergesort, and Heap sort, together with selection algorithms. The treatment concludes with the study of graphs, introducing common graph representations, traversal algorithms, and, in the case of weighted graphs, algorithms for computing minimum spanning trees.

databases.title: Database Systems
databases.subtitle: Models, languages and design of information systems.
databases.overview:
Database systems introduces the fundamental principles of information systems and database management systems, analyzing the conceptual, logical, and physical models used for data representation and management. The treatment begins with the relational model, introducing the notion of relation and the main integrity constraints.

Relational algebra is then presented as a formal language for querying data, analyzing fundamental operations such as union, intersection, difference, selection, projection, and join. On this basis, the SQL language is studied, including data types, table creation, integrity constraint specification, and data querying through the SELECT statement, with grouping, ordering, aggregate operators, nested queries, and views.

A significant part is devoted to database design. The Entity–Relationship model is introduced as a tool for conceptual design, addressing entities, relationships, attributes, cardinalities, and generalizations. Logical design follows, with the analysis of redundancies, restructuring of ER schemas, and translation into the relational model.

It continues with the study of normal forms and functional dependencies, introducing decomposition techniques, minimal covers, and normalization procedures up to third normal form and Boyce–Codd normal form. Advanced topics such as active databases, triggers, and transaction management are also addressed. The use of a real system, such as PostgreSQL, provides practical case studies to contextualize the theoretical concepts.

introCs.title: Foundations of Computer Science
introCs.subtitle: Information representation, programming, and data structures.
introCs.overview:
Foundations of computer science provide a systematic view of the principles underlying computing systems and programming. It introduces low-level representation of information, analyzing numerical data encoding, instruction representation, and processor architecture. Particular attention is devoted to the C programming language as a tool for understanding the relationship between software and hardware, including the processes of compilation, assembly, and execution.

The fundamental concepts that characterize a programming language are then introduced, including syntax, formal grammar, semantics, and syntactic structures. The C language is studied in depth, covering data types, variables and constants, operators and expressions, pointers, arrays, control statements, functions, and structured data.

It continues with the study of elementary data structures and associated programming paradigms, addressing lists in their different representations, as well as iteration and recursion. In this context, the C++ language is introduced, with particular reference to object-oriented programming, including classes and objects, data abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism, virtual functions, generic programming, and exception handling.

The treatment is completed with an analysis of the fundamental mechanisms of object-oriented programming, such as encapsulation, delegation, substitutability, and resource management. Finally, the principles underlying design patterns and programming idioms are introduced, with reference to recurring solutions such as RAII, Observer, Factory, Singleton, and Adapter.

computerArchitecture.title: Computer Architecture
computerArchitecture.subtitle: Digital circuits, CPUs, pipelines, and memory.
computerArchitecture.overview:
Computer architecture introduces the principles behind the design of computing systems and their operation at the hardware level. The subject begins with the analysis of modern computers and the evolution of technology, focusing on the role of performance and the criteria used to evaluate architectures.

It covers combinational logic networks, with particular attention to specification, synthesis, and minimization. The course also addresses timing methodologies and memory elements, as well as finite-state machines and sequential networks, which describe the dynamic behavior of digital systems.

The curriculum introduces the assembly language of the RISC-V system and its simulator, with a laboratory dedicated to assembly programming. Fundamental concepts such as number representation, binary arithmetic, ALU design, multiplication, division, and floating-point numbers are discussed in depth.

A central part is devoted to the RISC-V processor, including the design of a single-cycle CPU, the data path, and the control unit. The subject then examines performance improvements through pipelining, analyzing pipeline hazards and the mechanisms used to solve them, including exceptions and processor enhancements.

The treatment concludes with memory hierarchies, cache organization, and an introduction to virtual memory, providing a complete view of modern computing systems.

programming.title: Programming
programming.subtitle: From problems to programs, with Java.
programming.overview:
Programming introduces the computational way of thinking and the tools needed to turn a problem into an executable solution. The course begins by distinguishing algorithms from programs and by using representation and decomposition to break complex problems into simpler parts.

It also introduces complexity analysis, providing the basic tools needed to estimate the cost of a solution and compare different approaches. On this foundation, procedural programming is studied through the organization of code around instructions, data, and well-defined procedures.

Java is used as the main programming language. The course covers primitive types, variables, expressions, and basic operations, then moves to control flow through conditional and iterative structures.

The treatment concludes with methods, which make programs clearer and reusable, and recursion, with attention to how recursive calls work, how base cases are defined, and how they lead to a correct solution.

objectOrientedProgramming.title: Object-Oriented Programming
objectOrientedProgramming.subtitle: Classes, relationships, and reusable structures.
objectOrientedProgramming.overview:
Object-oriented programming introduces a way of designing software around objects that combine data and behavior. The course begins with the foundations of the paradigm, clarifying the role of classes, objects, state, behavior, and responsibilities.

It then explores classes and objects in more detail, together with the mechanisms used to describe relationships between different types. Interfaces and inheritance are presented as tools for defining contracts, reusing code, and building flexible hierarchies while keeping what an object does separate from how it does it.

The treatment also covers exception handling, which is used to represent and manage abnormal situations without mixing error paths with the normal flow of a program. It then introduces generic programming, allowing reusable components to work with different types while preserving type safety.

The final part focuses on data structures and collections, with attention to how groups of objects are organized, traversed, and manipulated in object-oriented programs.

linearAlgebra.title: Linear Algebra and Geometry
linearAlgebra.subtitle: Vector spaces, matrices, and linear transformations.
linearAlgebra.overview:
Linear algebra and geometry introduces the fundamental mathematical structures used to describe and analyze linear systems in scientific and engineering contexts. The treatment begins with the study of Euclidean spaces and vectors, addressing coordinates, scalar and vector products, and the tools of analytic geometry in space.

Linear systems and their representation through matrices are then introduced, with particular emphasis on the Gaussian elimination method as a fundamental tool for solving systems and analyzing their properties. Matrix algebra is developed systematically, including basic operations, invertible matrices, and the computation of the inverse.

It continues with the study of vector spaces and linear transformations, introducing concepts such as kernel and image, generators and linear independence, dimension and rank. In this framework, the representation theorem, the rank–nullity theorem, and Grassmann’s formula are presented.

A central part is devoted to determinants, their properties and computational techniques, including Laplace expansions and the Binet theorem, as well as the relationship between determinant and rank. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are subsequently introduced, together with the study of similar matrices and the problem of canonical forms.

The treatment concludes with the study of Euclidean spaces and orthogonal structures, including orthonormal bases, orthogonal matrices, orthogonal projections, and the Gram–Schmidt algorithm, leading to the method of least squares. Finally, spectral theorems, both in the real and complex cases and the study of quadratic forms are presented.

discreteMathLogic.title: Discrete Mathematics and Logic
discreteMathLogic.subtitle: Sets, relations, discrete structures, and formal reasoning.
discreteMathLogic.overview:
Discrete mathematics and logic introduces the mathematical structures and proof techniques used to reason about finite or countable objects, which are central to information theory, computer science, and formal logic. The course begins with sets, set operations, and relations between elements, including order and equivalence relations and their role in modeling structured data.

It then develops the basic tools of proof, such as induction and recursive definitions, with applications to sequences, arithmetic constructions, and combinatorial problems. Modular arithmetic is also introduced, including greatest common divisors, the Euclidean algorithm, Bézout’s identity, prime numbers, and Diophantine equations.

A large part of the course is devoted to combinatorics, including permutations, arrangements, combinations, inclusion-exclusion, Euler’s totient function, and applications to RSA cryptography. The subject then moves to polynomials with integer and rational coefficients, algebraic structures such as groups, rings, and fields, and the symmetric group and its fundamental properties.

The course concludes with graph theory and mathematical logic: paths, trees, connectivity, Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs, planar and bipartite graphs, graph coloring, Hall’s theorem, Menger’s theorem, and flow networks. The final part introduces propositional and predicate logic, skolemization, and automated deduction, providing the foundations for formal reasoning and verification.

analysis.title: Mathematical Analysis
analysis.subtitle: Real numbers, functions and infinitesimal calculus.
analysis.overview:
Mathematical analysis provides the theoretical foundations of infinitesimal calculus and the study of real-valued functions. The treatment begins with real numbers and their algebraic and order properties, introducing the concepts of supremum and infimum and the axiom of completeness as the basis of analysis.

The language and syntax of mathematics are then introduced, together with basic set theory and elementary logic, which are essential for the rigorous formulation of mathematical results. The study of real functions and their graphs forms the starting point for the analysis of limits, continuity, and differentiability.

A central part is devoted to differential calculus in one variable, with applications to the qualitative study of functions and optimization problems. This is followed by the introduction of the Riemann integral and the fundamental theorem of calculus, which establishes the connection between differentiation and integration.

It also addresses the study of convex functions, Taylor’s formula, and asymptotic expansions as tools for function approximation. The treatment is completed with an introduction to ordinary differential equations, numerical sequences, and series, providing an essential foundation for further developments in analysis and its applications.

networking.title: Networking
networking.subtitle: Principles of data communication and computer networks.
networking.overview:
Networking studies the fundamental principles governing the transmission of information between interconnected computing systems. The subject introduces the concept of information and its measurement, the main network topologies, and the role of protocols as sets of rules that regulate communication between distributed entities.

A significant part is devoted to data transmission, analyzing the nature of analog and digital signals, modulation and multiplexing techniques, the operation of modems, and communication interfaces. Issues related to coding, transmission errors, and the distinction between synchronous and asynchronous systems are also addressed.

The study of computer networks continues with the analysis of network structures, distinguishing between switched and dedicated networks, point-to-point and multipoint systems, and the main types of wide area networks (WANs). In this context, the ISO/OSI model is introduced as a conceptual framework for the design and analysis of network protocols.

Particular attention is given to the lower and intermediate layers of the ISO/OSI stack. The data link layer is examined through the specifications of data link control protocols, including BSC, HDLC, SDLC, and PPP. The network layer addresses the IP protocol, the definition of subnets and interfaces, and routing configuration mechanisms, both static and dynamic.

The treatment is completed with the study of network services, including name management through host tables and DNS, access to network resources, and electronic mail services. Finally, the main aspects of network management and security are introduced, with reference to risk assessment, access control, firewalls, TCP wrappers, and network monitoring tools.

content.whyComputersTitle: Why computers don't speak like us
whyComputers: A computer does not operate on concepts like letters, words, or meanings: it works exclusively on measurable physical phenomena. At the core of any digital system are electrical circuits, through which data is transmitted and stored. A real circuit can be in 2 fundamental states: closed (current flows) or open (no current).
This concept becomes clearer by observing what happens in a real circuit.

In hardware, these 2 conditions are realized and recognized through voltage levels: the presence of a voltage above a certain threshold indicates a closed circuit, while absence (or a very low voltage) indicates an open circuit. Unlike the analog world, where values can vary continuously, these states are discretized, i.e., intentionally reduced to a finite number of possibilities.
We can now see how a continuous voltage is transformed into only two states.

The choice to use only two distinct states is not random. Two-level systems (open/closed circuit, low/high voltage) are: easier to design, more stable over time, less sensitive to electrical noise and environmental variations.

In the presence of disturbances, it is much easier to correctly distinguish two well-separated states than many intermediate levels. For this reason, the physical behavior of the circuit is represented abstractly by associating these two states with two conventional symbols: 0 and 1. This gives birth to the binary system, which is the basis of all computer operation.

The single binary symbol, 0 or 1, is called a bit (contraction of binary digit). The bit represents the smallest unit of information that a digital system can handle: a choice between two mutually exclusive alternatives, directly connected to the physical state of an electronic circuit.
bitsBytes: To make information management easier, bits are not treated individually but grouped into fixed-size units. The most common unit is the byte, now defined as a sequence of 8 bits.
A byte is not just an abstract concept: we can build it manually.

Historically, the term byte simply referred to a group of bits and did not have a universal size: in early architectures it could vary depending on the hardware design. Standardization on 8 bits gradually emerged because this size was adequate for several fundamental purposes.

A group of 8 bits can represent 2⁸ = 256 distinct configurations, enough to: encode a complete set of basic textual characters, represent small numerical values without more complex structures, efficiently address portions of memory.

Furthermore, many computer architectures are designed so that memory is addressed by byte, not by individual bits: each memory address refers to an 8-bit cell. This simplifies hardware design, memory management, and interaction with input/output devices.
content.numbersToSymbolsTitle: From numbers to symbols: character encoding
numbersToSymbols: At this point, a crucial problem arises: if the computer stores and manipulates only binary numbers, how can it represent abstract symbols like letters, digits or punctuation marks? The answer is encoding: a shared convention that establishes a correspondence between: a graphic symbol, a numeric value, a sequence of bits.
In other words, a letter is not seen by the computer as a letter, but as a number to which we assign a symbolic meaning.
dataRepresentation: When writing a program, one of the fundamental problems is to determine how to represent information inside the computer. Any data processed by software, regardless of its complexity, must be translated into a form compatible with hardware, i.e., sequences of bits.
Conceptually, the data manipulated by a program can be reduced to two main categories: data representing numeric values, data representing textual or symbolic information.
These two categories also reflect the way information is traditionally recorded and transmitted in human culture: through numbers and symbols.
numericTypes: In the C language, the distinction between numbers is explicit and assigned to well-defined types, including: int, float, double.

In all these cases, what the computer stores is not the number as an abstract mathematical concept, but a binary encoding that represents or approximates that value according to precise rules defined by the language and architecture.
content.charTypeTitle: The char type and character encoding
charType: In programming languages, a single character is represented using the char type. A char does not directly contain a letter, but a numeric value.

The meaning of this value depends on a character encoding table, which establishes the association between numbers and graphic symbols. In an encoding like ASCII, for example, a certain numeric value corresponds to the letter 'A', another to the letter 'B', and so on.
conventions: In general, data representation inside a computer results from the combination of multiple formal conventions, including: the positionality of the encoding, the number base used, the number of digits employed, sign encoding for negative numbers, representation of fractional parts and rational values.
positionalCoding: To represent numbers, number systems use a finite set of elementary digits, called the base. In daily life, we are accustomed to the decimal base, which uses digits from 0 to 9. With these digits, it is possible to represent the first ten values directly; to represent larger numbers, sequences of digits are used.

In a positional numbering system, the meaning of a digit does not depend solely on its value but also on its position within the number. For this reason, numbers made up of the same digits but arranged in a different order represent different values: for example, 125 and 315 do not indicate the same quantity.

Each position within the number is associated with a weight, which depends on the base of the numbering system. Moving from right to left, the weight of the digits increases regularly, according to the chosen base. The rightmost digit is called the least significant digit, while the leftmost is the most significant digit.

why_this_course.title: Course objective
why_this_course.p1: Imagine working at a company that manages billions of data. A colleague proposes an idea to sort this data faster. How do you know if their idea is truly better than the current solution? How do you predict how long it will take to get the results?
why_this_course.p2_intro: You can't wait to run the program and time it: there's too much data, computers vary, timing depends on thousands of external factors.
why_this_course.p3_intro: What you need is a mathematical tool that allows you to:
why_this_course.p2_item1: Compare the speed of different algorithms
why_this_course.p2_item2: Predict how an algorithm behaves as data grows
why_this_course.p2_item3: choose the best algorithm for your problem

chapter1.title: What Are Algorithms and Why They Matter

subsection1.title: Computational Problem
subsection1.p1: Given an input domain I and an output domain O, a computational problem is a mathematical relation
subsection1.p3: that associates with each element x ∈ I one or more elements y ∈ O such that (x,y) ∈ R.
subsection1.p4: For each input instance x, the problem consists in determining one (or all) elements y of the output domain that are related to x according to R.

subsection2.title: Algorithm
subsection2.p1: Given a computational problem, an algorithm is a finite and effective procedure, consisting of a set of elementary and well-defined instructions, expressed in a formal system of computation, that transforms a set of input data into a set of output data representing the solution to the problem, in finite time.
subsection2.p2: For an ordered sequence of actions to be considered a true algorithm, it must satisfy some fundamental properties. In particular, an algorithm must be:
subsection2.p2_item1: General: applicable to all possible instances of the problem, not just specific cases.
subsection2.p2_item2: Finite: must terminate after a limited number of steps.
subsection2.p2_item3: Unambiguous: each instruction must be clear and interpretable in a unique way.
subsection2.p2_item4: Complete/Robust: must account for every possible input data situation and behave correctly in all cases.
subsection2.p2_item5: Deterministic: starting from the same input data, must always produce the same output data.
subsection2.p2_item6: Executable: must be possible to identify an executor (human or machine) capable of performing all the planned actions.
subsection2.p2_item7: Effective: must lead to the problem's solution optimally, both in terms of execution time and memory usage.

section2.title: A bit of history
section2.p1_item1: Algorithms have ancient roots, already present in Egyptian and Babylonian mathematical texts:
section2.p1_item1_children_0: Rhind Papyrus (ca. 1850 BC): contains an algorithm for multiplication.
section2.p1_item1_children_1: Babylonian and Indian mathematicians developed numerical and geometric algorithms (calculation of tangents, angle bisection, greatest common divisor with Euclid).
section2.p2_item2: The term algorithm derives from Abu Abdullah Muhammad bin Musa al-Khwarizmi (VIII–IX century), a mathematician and scholar of Baghdad:
section2.p2_item2_children_0: His most famous work: Al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala (ca. 820 AD), translated into Latin as Liber algebrae et almucabala.
section2.p2_item2_children_1: He introduced Indian (Arabic) numerals to the West and concepts of systematic computation.
section2.p2_item2_children_2: The term "algorithm" is born from his name, while "zero" and "digit" derive from sifr, the Arabic numeral 0.

section3.title: Examples of Computational Problems and Algorithms

list.definition:
Let S = {s₀, s₁, ..., sₙ₋₁} be a set of elements and t ∈ S a target element. Deleting t from S consists of returning a set S' = S \ {t} that no longer contains t.
S' = S \ {t}
list.algorithm: Iterate through all elements of S; if you find an element equal to t, remove it from the set. At the end, return S'.

list.definition:
Let S = {s₀, s₁, ..., sₙ₋₁} be a set of elements. Sorting S consists of producing a set S' = {s'₀, s'₁, ..., s'ₙ₋₁} such that s'₀ ≤ s'₁ ≤ ... ≤ s'ₙ₋₁ according to a predefined criterion.
Sort(S) = S' with s'₀ ≤ s'₁ ≤ ... ≤ s'ₙ₋₁
list.algorithm: For example, with Bubble Sort: compare pairs of adjacent elements and swap them if they're in the wrong order; repeat until S' is completely sorted.

list.definition:
Let A = a₀, a₁, ..., aₙ₋₁ be a sorted sequence of distinct data. Searching for a value v in A consists of finding an index i such that 0 ≤ i ≤ n−1 if v = aᵢ, or returning −1 if v is not present.
lookup(A,v) = i, ∃i ∈ {0,...,n−1} : aᵢ = v; −1 otherwise
list.algorithm: To find v in A, compare v with each element in sequence; return the corresponding index if found, otherwise −1. Alternatively, if A is sorted, you can use Binary Search to optimize the search time.

list.definition:
Let A = a₀, a₁, ..., aₙ₋₁ be a sequence of comparable data. Finding the maximum in A consists of determining the element m ∈ A such that m ≥ aᵢ for all i ∈ {0,...,n−1}.
max(A) = m where m ≥ aᵢ ∀i ∈ {0,...,n−1}
list.algorithm: Initialize m = a₀; iterate through elements from a₁ to aₙ₋₁; if you find an element greater than m, update m. At the end, return m.

section1.title: Why Natural Language Is Not Enough
section1.p1: Descriptions of algorithms in natural language are often imprecise and ambiguous, because natural language is not designed to express procedures rigorously and unambiguously. In natural language, words and phrases can have multiple meanings and leave doubts about the exact sequence of steps to follow, making it difficult to analyze or implement the algorithm.
section1.p2: To overcome these limitations, it is necessary to adopt more formal and systematic descriptions:
section1.p2_item1_children_0: Formal methods such as pseudo-code or mathematical formalisms allow describing algorithms with a level of detail that is unambiguous and interpretable by both humans and, with translation to code, by machines.
section1.p2_item1_children_1: Formalization makes logical constructs, conditions, and iterations explicit in a manner similar to the structure of programming languages, but independent of any specific language.

section2.title: Pseudo-code
section2.p1: Pseudo-code is a language for describing algorithms that stands halfway between natural language and a programming language. It does not have rigid syntax like programming languages, but uses structured constructs (assignments, conditionals, loops) to represent the steps of the algorithm in a clear and readable way.

section3.title: Pseudo-code Symbols
section3.p1: Below you will find a complete guide with the fundamental symbols and constructs of pseudo-code. The table shows each element of the syntax, a brief description of its meaning, and an example of use.

items.description: Variable declaration with specified type (integer, integer[] for arrays)
items.example: variable i: integer ← 0 / variable arr: integer[]

items.description: Assignment: assigns the value of an expression to a variable
For loop: repeats from 0 to range
items.example: for i to n-1 do ... end for

items.description: While loop: repeats while condition is true
items.example: while i < n do ... end while

items.description: Conditional: executes different blocks based on condition
items.example: if x > 0 then ... else ... end if

items.description: Returns a value and terminates the function
Access to the i-th element of array A
Function definition with typed parameters and return type
items.example: function max(A: integer[], n: integer) → integer

section1.title: Correctness
section1.p1_item1: it always produces the expected result
section1.p1_item2: it terminates in a finite number of steps
section1.p2_item2: or with a rigorous but informal description, arguing why each step is valid
section1.p3_item1: there are problems that cannot be solved (undecidable problems)
section1.p3_item2: there are problems that can only be solved approximately
section1.p3_item3: for some problems there is a theoretical limit: beyond a certain efficiency it is not possible to go

section2.title: Efficiency
section2.p1: Once we establish that the algorithm works, we need to understand how much it 'costs' to run it.
section2.p2: This is where algorithmic complexity comes in.

section3.title: What is Complexity?
section3.p1: It is the study of the resources that an algorithm consumes as a function of:
section3.p2_item1: Time: how long it takes to complete execution
section3.p2_item2: Space: how much memory it uses during execution
section3.p2_item3: Bandwidth: how much data it needs to transmit (in the case of distributed algorithms)

chapter4.title: Evaluating Algorithms - Correctness
chapter4.p1: When we say that an algorithm is correct, it's not enough that it "seems to work".
chapter4.p2: A formal reasoning is needed to prove that:
chapter4.p2_item1: it always produces the correct result
chapter4.p3: One of the most powerful tools for proving the correctness of iterative algorithms is the concept of invariant.

section1.title: What is an invariant?
section1.p1: An invariant is a property that remains true during the execution of a part of the program.

subsection1.title: Loop Invariant
subsection1.p1: It is a condition that holds true every time control enters the loop, i.e., immediately before the execution of the loop body.
subsection1.p2: When we talk about "beginning of the iteration" we mean the moment when the loop guard is true and the body is about to be executed.

subsection2.title: Class Invariant
subsection2.p1: In the context of object-oriented programming, it is a property that must be true before and after the execution of every public method, i.e., at the end of every externally visible operation.
subsection2.p2: Example: in a class representing a queue, a possible invariant is:
subsection2.p3: This property must always be satisfied after any operation (enqueue, dequeue, etc.).

section2.title: How to use an invariant to prove correctness?
section2.p1: The structure of the proof resembles mathematical induction and involves three fundamental steps:
section2.step1_text: Prove that the invariant is true before the first iteration.
section2.step2_text: Prove that: if the invariant is true before an iteration, then it remains true after the execution of the loop body.
section2.step3_text: When the loop terminates, the exit condition combined with the invariant must imply the correctness of the algorithm. In other words, the invariant, at the moment of exit, must become the property we wanted to prove.

section3.title: Example: Computing the Maximum
section3.pseudocode:
function max(A: integer[], n: integer) → integer
    variable maxSoFar: integer ← A[0]
    variable i: integer
    for i ← 1 to n-1 do
        if A[i] > maxSoFar then
            maxSoFar ← A[i]
    return maxSoFar
section3.invariant_text: At the beginning of each iteration with index i, maxSoFar contains the maximum of elements A[0 ... i-1].
section3.init_text: Before the first iteration (i = 1): maxSoFar = A[0]. So it is indeed the maximum of A[0 ... 0]. The invariant holds.
section3.conservation_text: If before iteration i the partial maximum is correct, we compare A[i] and update if necessary. So at the end of iteration i, maxSoFar is the maximum of A[0 ... i]. The invariant is preserved.
section3.conclusion_text: When the loop terminates (i = n), maxSoFar is the maximum of A[0 ... n-1]. Therefore the algorithm is correct.

section4.title: Correctness of Recursive Algorithms
section4.p1: For recursive algorithms, instead of loop invariants, we directly use induction on input size.

subsection1.title: Example: Recursive Binary Search
subsection1.pseudocode:
function binarySearch(A: integer[], v: integer, start: integer, end: integer) → integer
    if start > end then
        return -1
    variable m: integer ← floor((start + end)/2)
    if A[m] == v then
        return m
    else if A[m] < v then
        return binarySearch(A, v, m+1, end)
    else
        return binarySearch(A, v, start, m-1)
subsection1.p1: The proof is done by induction on the size of the subarray n = end - start + 1.
subsection1.base_text: If n = 0 (i.e., start > end), the function returns -1, which is correct.
subsection1.hypothesis_text: Assume that the algorithm is correct for all inputs of size less than n.
subsection1.step_text: For an array of size n: if we find the element at the center → correct. Otherwise we recursively call on a smaller subarray. By the inductive hypothesis, that call is correct. Therefore the case of size n is also correct.
